title: AI agents explained: What they are and how they work
text:
Learning hub>Agentic AI>What are AI agents?What are AI agents? A guide covering how they work, different types, and real examplesSep 8, 2026|13 min readAn AI agent is a software system that receives a user-defined goal, breaks it into steps, and executes those steps using tools, data, and context, operating under a user’s direction and oversight. It can carry out the multi-step tasks and actions needed to reach that goal, adjusting as it goes.The distinction between AI agents and the bots or assistants you may already use is important. AI agents represent a shift from tools that respond to tools that execute on your behalf, while you stay in control of the outcome.Today’s AI assistants already help with everyday tasks such as searching the web, drafting content, and problem-solving. AI agents build on that foundation by taking actions inside the apps and accounts you already use. That might mean drafting and sending an email, adding an event to your calendar, or pulling together options for a purchase based on both your instructions and what it already knows about your preferences. It sequences those steps itself instead of waiting for you at every turn. These are still emerging systems that work best when users review and guide their output.This guide breaks down what AI agents are, how they work under a user’s direction and oversight, and why they’re shaping the next wave of everyday AI use.What are AI agents and how do they work?If you’re looking for an AI agent definition, here’s the simplest version: An AI agent is an artificial intelligence system designed to process goals, plan steps, and execute actions across tools on a user's behalf.Unlike traditional chatbots that respond to one prompt at a time, AI agents can keep tasks moving across multiple steps without requiring input at each stage. Take a prompt like “clean up my inbox.” Given permission to read and act in your email, an agent can sort what is there, pull dates and deadlines onto your calendar, surface the messages most likely to matter, and draft replies for you to review before anything sends. One instruction, several steps, and you approve what goes out.That approval step is the part to hold onto. Reviewing what an agent produces before anything is finalized helps keep the outcome in your hands.But, how do AI agents really work? It comes down to a few key components.A core powered by large language modelsAt the center of most modern AI agents are LLMs, which serve as the system’s central processing component. They read your request, take in the information around it, and generate a response. They also support step-by-step processing, so the system can decide what to do next based on your original request and what it has already found, rather than treating every step as a fresh, unrelated question. This is what turns a single instruction like “clean up my inbox” into a sequence: read what is there, work out what matters, then draft replies, in that order.Memory and context that persist over timeAI agents are not limited to a single exchange. Many draw on two kinds of information: what you have said earlier in the conversation you are having, and details saved over time, like your preferences or past requests. So if you have already flagged that messages from your child’s school always matter, an agent can apply that the next time it sorts your inbox without being told again.Planning and task breakdownOnce a goal is specified, an AI agent can break it down into smaller steps: sequencing tasks, comparing options against defined criteria, and selecting a next action without requiring input at each step. This capacity to process tasks in stages and select actions is what distinguishes AI agents from more rigid automation tools.The AI agent systems that users are likely to interact with are typically composed of sub-agents, so that the AI agent system can work on different parts of a goal at the same time, or even different goals at the same time.Tools, APIs, and the ability to take actionAI agents connect to external tools and systems through application programming interfaces (APIs), so their output is not limited to text. Through these connections, the system can update data, organize information, add a calendar item derived from an email, or trigger automation across different workflows.Behind the scenes, it all runs in a continuous loop: the agent receives input, processes it, performs an action, evaluates the result, and adjusts if needed. This cycle lets AI agents operate independently based on users’ prompts and refine their output over time.Four types of AI agentsAI agents aren't all built the same. Agentic capabilities exist on a spectrum, with some only able to execute simple actions, while others can plan, learn, and take action in more complex environments. Most AI agents don't fit neatly into a single category, and AI agent systems may utilize different kinds of agents to help achieve components of a task. These agent-types are best understood as design patterns that feed into agentic products and systems, not boxes each agent has to fit into.Here are the main types of agents, with real-world examples.1. Reactive agentsThese agents respond to what’s happening right now. They’re connected to external tools and data sources, which means they can act on live information. For example, a reactive agent might flag an unusual charge on your account the moment it appears, or check real-time inventory before confirming an order.2. Goal-based agentsThese agents are driven by specific outcomes. The system evaluates possible actions and selects the one most likely to achieve or advance toward the goal. The goal becomes the anchor for every action the system takes. Say you tell an agent you want to be ready to run a half marathon in ten weeks: that goal is what it measures each decision against, from what this week’s runs look like to what happens when you miss one.3. Utility-based agentsThese agents don’t simply ask the baseline question, “Does this reach the goal?” They take it a step further, asking, “What’s the best possible outcome?” The system weighs different options given the instructions it has received from the user and its training and selects the one that delivers the highest overall value, especially when trade-offs are involved. Tell an agent you want to add plants to a patio that gets partial sun and attracts butterflies. It narrows down the plants that will do well in your conditions, then tells you where to find them nearby.4. Learning agentsLearning agents are the most adaptive type of AI agent. These systems improve over time by analyzing the results of prior actions and using feedback to adjust subsequent behavior. The more they’re used, and the more they learn about you, the better they become. Many of the AI systems people interact with today fall into this category. For example, if you get migraines and can’t work out what sets them off, you can ask an agent to track them with you. You tell it what was going on and when it starts, and it builds on each entry, eventually pointing to a pattern you hadn’t noticed before.Three benefits of using AI agentsThe real value of AI agents is that they take repetitive, time-consuming tasks off your plate. Instead of managing every step yourself, an AI agent handles the legwork and surfaces what you need to make the final call. By removing routine busywork, agents free up headspace for the things that actually need your attention.Here are three benefits that stand out.1. Get time back on everyday tasksDaily life is full of necessary but time-consuming tasks, whether it’s sorting your inbox to find the three personal messages that actually need a reply, catching a free trial before it quietly converts to a monthly charge, or pulling calendars from three different apps into one view so you stop double-booking yourself. AI agents can handle these bounded, concrete tasks in the background, reducing the need for manual reminders or follow-up. You stay in control of the final decision.According to data from the U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics, Americans spend over two hours a day on household tasks alone, and that’s before factoring in shopping and other personal admin tasks. A PwC report estimates that figure may be closer to four hours daily, and finds that AI-enabled household support could deliver up to $330 billion in socioeconomic value. AI agents chip away at that load, freeing up more time for the things that need your judgment.2. Help across the full arc of a taskMost tools can only do one thing at a time, but AI agents are different. They can own an entire process, end to end. They receive a request, break it into steps, execute each one, check results, and adjust when things don’t go as planned.Say you need to sell a piece of furniture. An agent can research local pricing, draft the listing, and queue up buyer replies for your review. Or take booking a birthday dinner: the agent compares spots that fit your group size, budget, and date, then shares a restaurant recommendation for you to confirm. Each job is bounded, easy to evaluate, and stays under your control.3. Less cognitive load, clearer decisionsGood decisions take time, especially when you’re sorting through large amounts of information on your own. AI agents can process large amounts of information, filter for relevance, and surface key details quickly.Whether you’re trying to work out where your money actually goes each month or vetting three weekend hike options near you with travel times, AI agents reduce the cognitive load of sorting through options so you can act on what matters.Understanding the limitations: risks and responsible useAI agents are a powerful new category of technology, but they are still emerging systems with real limitations. Like all AI, they can make mistakes, misinterpret instructions, or produce inaccurate outputs. Because agents can take actions (not just generate text), errors may have more tangible consequences than a wrong answer in a chat.Key considerations to keep in mind:Accuracy and reliability. AI agents may produce incorrect or incomplete results, especially with complex or ambiguous tasks. Always verify important outputs before acting on them.Security and data access. An agent can only reach the accounts and apps you connect it to, so it is worth being deliberate about which ones you grant. Start with the connections you need for the task in front of you, check what permissions you have granted, and remove access you are no longer using.Human oversight matters. The simplest way to keep oversight is to ask. You can tell an agent to walk you through what it did, explain why it made a choice, or show you something before it goes out.These systems are still maturing. AI agent technology is evolving quickly, but it is not infallible. Expect occasional failures, and ask it to perform tasks where you are comfortable with failure if it happens. As you see where an agent is reliable, you can hand off more.The best approach to AI agents is one of informed experimentation: use them to save time and reduce effort, but maintain the oversight that helps you stay in control of outcomes.What’s the difference between AI agents, AI assistants, and bots?The difference between AI agents, AI assistants, and bots comes down to how independently they can think, plan, and take action.Some systems simply react to inputs, while others help you complete tasks step by step. A newer category, agentic AI systems, can operate more independently, executing workflows with less manual input at each stage. Because these systems can take actions on a user’s behalf, it’s important to review and monitor what your agent is doing, especially as you learn how it handles different types of tasks.Here’s how they compare.TYPEHOW IT WORKSLEVEL OF CAPABILITYWHAT IT'S BEST FOREXAMPLEBotsFollow fixed rules and respond to specific inputsLowSimple, repetitive tasksFAQ bots and spam filtersPrompt-based AI assistantsRespond to prompts and help complete tasks step by step

MediumWriting, searching, and organizing informationAI assistants that search, draft, and summarizeAI agentsAchieve user-set goals, break tasks into steps, and execute tasks HighMulti-step workflows and automationAn agent that handles a product return start to finish: looking up the order, checking the policy, generating the label, and scheduling the pickup with your oversight and permissionKey difference: Agentic vs. non-agentic systemsThe easiest way to distinguish agentic from non-agentic systems is to look at how they handle complex tasks.Bots wait for a trigger and respond in a fixed, predefined way. AI assistants are more flexible, but they still rely on user input to guide the process step-by-step. You ask, they respond.AI agents work differently. Once a goal is set, the system can determine the necessary steps and continue executing, checking in when needed but without requiring direction at every turn.Simply put: bots follow rules, assistants follow instructions, and agents execute toward goals.How AI agents change the way everyday tasks get doneAI agents are already operating in the background of tools people use every day. Tools that prep your meeting agenda by pulling context from scattered emails and files, apps that log a meal from a single photo and tell you where it puts you for the day, and systems that draft a dispute letter when an unauthorized charge appears are all early examples of agentic behavior in action. Each handles one bounded job, shows you the result, and lets you make the final call.AI assistants are already moving in this direction. As agentic capabilities become more available across consumer AI products, these systems will handle more complex, multi-step tasks on your behalf, like a training plan that adjusts when you miss a day or sleep badly, a migraine tracker that spots the pattern you keep missing, or a savings goal that checks in weekly and tells you when you’re drifting. Users will remain in control, with the ability to review, adjust, and approve what the agent does.The progression from simple chatbots to assistants to agents reflects a broader shift in how people interact with AI. Each step has moved from “AI that responds” to “AI that executes,” and agent technology is still maturing. As these systems improve, the line between tools that help you think and tools that help you get things done will continue to narrow.Want to stay ahead of the shift?
